prompt: Which describes the relationship between wavefronts and rays?
options: Rays join points of equal amplitude
Rays are only defined for longitudinal waves
markscheme: **B.** A ray shows the direction of energy transfer and is always perpendicular to the wavefronts (lines joining points in phase).

prompt: Light passes from air into glass. What happens to its speed, frequency and wavelength?
options: speed decreases, frequency decreases, wavelength unchanged
speed unchanged, frequency decreases, wavelength decreases
speed decreases, frequency unchanged, wavelength decreases
speed decreases, frequency increases, wavelength decreases
markscheme: **C.** The frequency is fixed by the source and cannot change at the boundary; the speed falls, so $\lambda=\dfrac vf$ falls too. Some light is also reflected at the boundary.

prompt: Explain why you can hear someone talking around a corner but cannot see them.
markscheme: Diffraction is significant when the gap or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength **(R1)**; sound wavelengths (about 0.1–10 m) are similar to doorways, while light wavelengths (~500 nm) are far smaller, so light diffracts negligibly **(R1)**

prompt: Plane water waves travel from deep water into shallow water, where they are slower, crossing the boundary at an angle. Describe the wavefront–ray diagram.
markscheme:
Wavefronts are closer together in the shallow region (shorter wavelength, same frequency) **(A1)**

Wavefronts are continuous across the boundary but change direction, with the part of each wavefront that enters first slowing first **(A1)**

Rays (perpendicular to wavefronts) bend towards the normal in the shallow water **(A1)**

concept: Critical angle and total internal reflection
prompt:
**(a)** Calculate the critical angle for glass of refractive index 1.50 in air. **[1]**

**(b)** An optical fibre has a core of index 1.50 and cladding of index 1.46. Calculate the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary. **[2]**

**(c)** State the two conditions for total internal reflection. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\sin c=\dfrac{1}{1.50}\Rightarrow c=42^{\circ}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** $\sin c=\dfrac{1.46}{1.50}$ **(M1)** $\Rightarrow c=77^{\circ}$ **(A1)**

**(c)** Light travels from higher to lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle **(A1)**

prompt: Light in air strikes water (refractive index 1.33) at $40^{\circ}$ to the normal. Calculate the angle of refraction and the speed of light in the water ($c=3.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$).
A pulse of amplitude +3 cm and a pulse of amplitude −2 cm travel towards each other on a rope. What is the displacement where they fully overlap, and what happens afterwards?
markscheme: **B.** Displacements add algebraically: $3+(-2)=+1$ cm. After passing, each pulse continues unchanged.

prompt: Explain why the light from two car headlights does not produce a visible interference pattern.
markscheme: A stable pattern needs coherent sources, with a constant phase difference (and the same frequency) **(R1)**; light from two separate lamps is emitted randomly with rapidly changing phase, so any pattern changes too fast to observe **(R1)**

prompt: Two loudspeakers emit the same 680 Hz note in phase. Point P is 3.00 m from one speaker and 3.75 m from the other. Determine whether P is a point of loud or quiet sound. (Speed of sound $=340\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)
markscheme:
$\lambda=\dfrac{340}{680}=0.50$ m **(A1)**; path difference $0.75$ m $=1.5\lambda$ **(M1)**

A half-integer number of wavelengths: destructive interference, quiet **(A1)**

prompt: Two coherent sources are in phase. For destructive interference at a point, the path difference must be:
markscheme: **C.** $\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda$ — the waves arrive half a cycle out of phase.

prompt:
Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away.

**(a)** Calculate the fringe separation. **[2]**

**(b)** State the effect on the fringe separation of moving the slits closer together. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $s=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}=\dfrac{600\times10^{-9}\times2.0}{0.30\times10^{-3}}=4.0\times10^{-3}$ m **(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** $s\propto\dfrac1d$, so the fringes become further apart **(A1)**

prompt:
Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a single slit of width 0.10 mm onto a screen 2.0 m away.

**(a)** Calculate the angle to the first minimum. **[1]**

**(b)** Calculate the width of the central maximum on the screen. **[1]**

**(c)** State the effect of making the slit narrower. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\theta=\dfrac\lambda b=6.0\times10^{-3}$ rad **(A1)**

**(b)** $2D\theta=2\times2.0\times6.0\times10^{-3}=0.024$ m $=24$ mm **(A1)** — twice the width of the other maxima

**(c)** $\theta$ increases: the central maximum becomes wider (and dimmer) **(A1)**

prompt: In a double-slit experiment the slits are 0.30 mm apart and each slit is 0.10 mm wide. Explain why the third-order interference maximum is missing.
markscheme:
Interference maxima: $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$; single-slit minima: $b\sin\theta=m\lambda$ **(M1)**

For $n=3$: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, the first diffraction minimum **(M1)**

The single-slit envelope has zero intensity there, so the interference maximum is suppressed **(R1)**

prompt:
Light of wavelength 550 nm falls normally on a grating with 600 lines per mm.

**(a)** Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum. **[2]**

**(b)** Determine the highest order visible. **[1]**

**(c)** State one advantage of a grating over a double slit for measuring wavelengths. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $d=\dfrac{1}{600\times10^{3}}=1.67\times10^{-6}$ m **(A1)**; $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{d}=0.33$, $\theta=19^{\circ}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** $n\le\dfrac d\lambda=3.03$, so $n=3$ **(A1)**

**(c)** Maxima are much sharper and brighter, and widely spaced, so angles can be measured precisely **(A1)**
